questions.prompt: In the combined complexity of CQ evaluation, which components may vary with the input?
options: The database, query, and tuple being tested
Only the database, with the query fixed
Only the query, with the database and target tuple fixed
Only the output size; the database and query are excluded from the input
questions.explanation: Combined complexity includes the query in the input size. Data complexity, by contrast, fixes the query.

questions.prompt: What does data complexity hold fixed?
options: The database D
The query Q
Every result of Q
The number of rows in every table
questions.explanation: Q is fixed while the amount of data grows. Fixing D while varying Q would measure a different kind of complexity.

questions.prompt: Why does the lecture ask whether a tuple t belongs to Q(D), rather than always requiring the entire output to be printed?
options: A CQ cannot output more than one tuple
Membership lets us count the entire output in constant time
The output may be very large and obscure the difficulty of deciding membership
The output is always smaller than the query
questions.explanation: This separates the cost of deciding membership from the size of the output. The query still has an output, but printing it is not the task being measured.

questions.prompt: Which complexity result does the lecture state for CQ evaluation?
options: PTIME combined complexity but undecidable data complexity
NP-complete data complexity for every fixed Q
Constant time under both measures
NP-complete combined complexity and PTIME data complexity
questions.explanation: The two statements use different complexity measures, so they do not conflict. The combined-complexity result does not make evaluation of every fixed query NP-complete.

questions.prompt: A fixed query has k variables, and the data domain has n values. How does brute-force enumeration of n^k assignments grow with n?
options: Polynomially, because k is constant
Always exponentially in n, even with k fixed
In constant time
It cannot be checked in finite time
questions.explanation: A fixed exponent gives polynomial data complexity. When k varies as part of the input, this argument does not establish polynomial combined complexity.

questions.prompt: What is a natural YES certificate for CQ membership?
options: A low-cost execution plan without a matching assignment
A variable assignment satisfying every atom and the required head tuple
An assignment satisfying only the first atom
An output tuple without a way to satisfy the body atoms
questions.explanation: Guess-and-verify uses a homomorphism as the witness. An execution plan alone does not prove that a match exists.

questions.prompt: What must be checked to verify a candidate mapping h?
options: Only that h matches the first atom
Only that the number of variables equals the number of columns
That h(body) is contained in D and h(head) equals the tuple t
Only that h does not rename relations
questions.explanation: Both the complete body and the output tuple must match. Checking one atom or only the relation names can miss join constraints.

questions.prompt: What idea underlies the reduction from 3-colorability?
options: Mapping every vertex to the same color is always valid
Checking only whether the graph has exactly three vertices
Allowing the ends of an edge to share a color if the graph has a cycle
Mapping vertices to three colors so that every edge connects different colors
questions.explanation: A graph homomorphism into the triangle of colors represents a coloring. Giving the same color to both ends of an edge violates the required color difference.

questions.prompt: In the color-model database for an undirected graph, E contains pairs of different colors. Why is E(red,red) absent?
options: To forbid assigning the same color to both ends of an edge
To force every vertex to be red
To exclude every graph with a cycle
To guarantee exactly one match for every query
questions.explanation: Omitting self-loops rules out same-color edges. Cycles can still be three-colored, so excluding cycles is not the purpose.

questions.prompt: What does membership in NP mean here?
options: All witnesses are known to be findable in polynomial time
A correct, polynomial-size witness can be checked in polynomial time
P has been proved different from NP
Every instance requires exponential time
questions.explanation: An efficient verifier does not imply an efficient method for finding a witness. NP-completeness also does not establish an exponential lower bound for every input.

questions.prompt: What does CQ-Satisfiability ask?
options: Whether Q runs quickly on the current database
Whether Q has a nonempty result on every database
Whether some database D makes Q(D) nonempty
Whether Q is equivalent to every query with the same head
questions.explanation: Satisfiability asks whether at least one database gives the query an answer. It is neither a performance benchmark nor a claim about every database.

questions.prompt: What does CQ-Equivalence require?
options: The two queries give the same result on one sample database
The two queries have the same number of atoms
The two queries have the same head name
Q1(D)=Q2(D) for every database D
questions.explanation: Equivalence quantifies over every D. Matching results on a test dataset provide limited evidence, not a general proof.

questions.prompt: What does Q1⊆Q2 mean?
options: For every D, every answer to Q1 is also an answer to Q2
For every D, Q2(D) is a subset of Q1(D)
The body of Q1 being a subset of the body of Q2 always suffices, regardless of the heads
The queries have the same output on exactly one D
questions.explanation: Containment concerns result sets on every database, rather than the number of atoms or their execution order.

questions.prompt: Which containment checks together establish equivalence?
options: Only Q1⊆Q2
Q1⊆Q2 and Q2⊆Q1
Only checking that the canonical databases have the same number of facts
Q1⊆Q1 alone
questions.explanation: Inclusion in both directions gives equality. One direction alone only says that one query's answers are contained in the other's.

questions.prompt: According to the lecture, what is the general complexity of CQ-Containment and CQ-Equivalence?
options: Undecidable
Always constant time
NP-complete
PTIME simply because every CQ is satisfiable
questions.explanation: Easy satisfiability does not imply easy containment. The homomorphism theorem leads to the NP-completeness of these two problems.

questions.prompt: How is the canonical database D[Q] constructed?
options: Delete the body and keep the head as a fact
Replace all variables with the same constant, regardless of structure
Choose any database with the same relation names
Replace each variable with its own fresh constant and retain the body atoms
questions.explanation: Freezing variables as fresh constants preserves the query's structure. The construction is not random data sampling.

questions.prompt: Which is a canonical database for Q(x):-R(x,y),S(y)?
options: {R(cx,cy),S(cy)}, with cx and cy distinct fresh constants
{R(cx,cy),S(cz)}, with cy different from cz
{R(cx,cx)} without S
Only {Q(cx)}
questions.explanation: Every occurrence of y must become the same constant cy. D[Q] contains body facts, not merely a fact for the head.

questions.prompt: Why is every pure positive CQ satisfiable in the lecture's setting?
options: It is true on every database, including the empty one
Its own canonical database provides an immediate match
Every atom is a tautology
Every relation must contain every possible tuple
questions.explanation: The canonical database provides at least one suitable D. It does not imply that the query has an answer on every D.

questions.prompt: If Q contains the constant 'Hue', how does the canonical construction handle it?
options: Replace Hue with the fresh constant for variable x
Delete every atom containing Hue
Keep Hue unchanged
Replace Hue with NULL
questions.explanation: Only variables are frozen into fresh constants; existing constants must retain their meaning. Replacing Hue would change the query.

questions.prompt: Within which scope is the claim 'every CQ is satisfiable' justified here?
options: All SQL queries with arbitrary NOT and inequality conditions
Every query under any schema constraints
Every query containing a contradictory condition
Pure positive CQs, without additional constraints that introduce contradictions
questions.explanation: The canonical witness proves satisfiability in the CQ language considered here. Additional constraints or contradictory conditions outside that fragment can invalidate the argument.

questions.prompt: To prove Q1⊆Q2, in which direction does the homomorphism theorem seek a mapping?
options: From Q2 to Q1
From Q1 to Q2
From an arbitrary database to the head of Q1
Only from Q1 to itself
questions.explanation: The mapping direction is opposite to the containment direction. This is easy to reverse: a stronger body produces a smaller answer set.

questions.prompt: Let Q1(x):-R(x,y),S(y) and Q2(x):-R(x,y). Which inclusion always holds?
options: Q2⊆Q1
Q1⊆Q2
Q1 and Q2 are equivalent on every D
The queries are always disjoint, even when D contains matching R and S facts
questions.explanation: Every Q1 match includes the R match required by Q2. The reverse fails when an R fact has no matching S fact.

questions.prompt: What additional condition distinguishes a query homomorphism from a body homomorphism?
options: It must be a bijection on all variables
It must preserve the number of atoms
It must map the source head tuple to the target head tuple position by position
Only the body mapping matters; the output tuple can be ignored
questions.explanation: Preserving the output is essential. A valid body mapping that sends an output variable to the wrong variable does not establish containment for the same output tuples.

questions.prompt: For Q1(x):-R(x,y),S(y) and Q2(x):-R(x,y), which database disproves Q2⊆Q1?
options: The empty database
{R(a,b)}, with S empty
questions.explanation: With only R(a,b) and an empty S, a belongs to Q2's result but not Q1's. Databases containing S(b) make both queries return a and are not counterexamples.

questions.prompt: If h:Q2→Q1 and g matches Q1 into D, why does Q2 also have a suitable match?
options: The composition g∘h maps Q2's body into D and preserves the head
h must be invertible
Q2 must have fewer variables than Q1
All queries with the same arity are equivalent
questions.explanation: Composition proves the sufficient direction of the theorem. A homomorphism need not be invertible, and equal arity alone is insufficient.

questions.prompt: What is the stated goal of CQ minimization?
options: Find a query returning the fewest tuples, regardless of meaning
Find an equivalent CQ with the fewest atoms
Merge variables however possible, even if the output changes
Choose only the cheapest join order for the current database
questions.explanation: Minimization preserves semantics while reducing atoms and joins. Shrinking the result by adding conditions is a different task.

questions.prompt: For Q(x):-R(x,y),R(x,z), under set semantics and without inequality, can the second atom be removed?
options: No, because y and z must have different values
Only if the database contains one tuple
Yes; the mapping z↦y proves that it is redundant
Yes, but the head must change to Q(y)
questions.explanation: Existential variables with different names may have the same value, so one R witness can satisfy both atoms. There is no requirement that y≠z.

questions.prompt: Before removing an atom, why check that all head variables still occur in the remaining body?
options: To make every variable occur exactly twice in the body
To allow every output variable to be merged into a constant
To allow deletion based only on column counts, without checking equivalence
To keep the query safe and its output bound by the remaining body
questions.explanation: The only atom binding an output variable cannot simply be removed. The procedure does not require variables to occur exactly twice.

questions.prompt: Let Qold be the query before deleting an atom and Qnew the query afterward. Which nontrivial mapping must the algorithm check?
options: Qold→Qnew, preserving the head
Only Qnew→Qold, because it is always harder
Database→Qnew on one sample database
A mapping that sends every output variable to an arbitrary constant
questions.explanation: Qnew→Qold follows immediately because the remaining body is included in the old body. The reverse mapping Qold→Qnew is needed for equivalence; the head cannot be changed arbitrarily.

questions.prompt: Can S(x) be removed from Q(x):-R(x,y),S(x) while preserving equivalence on every D?
options: Yes, because S has only one column
No; a database containing only R(a,b) is a counterexample
Yes, because R already binds x, so S adds no condition
Yes, after renaming the existential variable y
questions.explanation: When S is empty, the original query does not return a, but the query after deletion does. Low arity does not make an atom redundant.

questions.prompt: According to the theorem, how are two minimal CQs that are both equivalent to Q related?
options: Their text must match character for character
They may differ arbitrarily in their numbers of atoms
They are isomorphic: the same up to variable renaming
They only need the same number of output tuples on one D
questions.explanation: Uniqueness is up to isomorphism, not byte-for-byte identity. Variable names may differ while the structure remains the same.

questions.prompt: What is the core of Q in this section?
options: A materialized table storing Q(D) for the current data
The set of atoms occurring exactly once in the query text
The constants of one particular database that makes Q true
A minimal CQ equivalent to Q, unique up to variable renaming
questions.explanation: The core is a semantically minimized representation of the query. It is not a materialized result on a particular D.

questions.prompt: Can Q(x):-R(x,y) and P(a):-R(a,b) be isomorphic when x,y,a,b are variables?
options: Yes; rename x↦a,y↦b while preserving the head position
No, because their query names differ
No, because their variable names differ
Only if x and a are constants
questions.explanation: Variable names are symbols. Renaming that preserves atoms and head positions establishes isomorphism; variables must not be confused with fixed constants.

questions.prompt: For Q(x):-R(x,y) and P(a):-R(b,a), with a and b variables, can variable renaming alone establish equivalence?
options: Yes, because each has one R atom of arity 2
No; the head is in a different R position, so an output-preserving renaming does not generally exist
Yes, because all one-atom queries are equivalent
Yes, if the head is ignored when checking isomorphism
questions.explanation: Q returns R's first component, whereas P returns its second. D={R(c,d)} with c different from d gives different outputs. Core isomorphism must preserve the head.

questions.prompt: Does the uniqueness theorem itself provide a polynomial-time minimization algorithm?
options: Yes; uniqueness makes every homomorphism check constant time
Yes; atoms can be deleted arbitrarily until only one remains
No; uniqueness of the result does not make every search step cheap
No; the theorem states that a query cannot be minimized
questions.explanation: A canonical result may still be hard to find. The procedure still requires homomorphism checks, which are difficult in general.
